entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18193"/><div sID="gen37630" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18193"/>8. Rather as Greek, "Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead." Remember Christ risen, so as to follow Him. As He was raised after death, so if thou wouldest share His risen "life," thou must now share His "death" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.11">2Ti 2:11</reference>). The Greek perfect passive participle, implies a permanent character acquired by Jesus as the risen Saviour, and our permanent interest in Him as such. Christ's resurrection is put prominently forward as being the truth now assailed (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.18">2Ti 2:18</reference>), and the one best calculated to stimulate Timothy to steadfastness in sharing Paul's sufferings for the Gospel's sake (see on <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.3">2Ti 2:3</reference>).<div eID="gen37630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37631" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the seed of David--</hi>The one and only genealogy (as contrasted with the "endless genealogies," <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.4">1Ti 1:4</reference>) worth thinking of, for it proves Jesus to be the Messiah. The absence of the article in the Greek, and this formula, "of the seed of David" (compare <reference osisRef="Rom.1.3">Ro 1:3</reference>), imply that the words were probably part of a recognized short oral creed. In His death He assured us of His humanity; by His resurrection, of His divinity. That He was not crucified for His own sin appears from His resurrection; that He was crucified shows that He bore sin, on Him, though not in Him.<div eID="gen37631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37632" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my gospel--</hi>that which I always taught. <div eID="gen37632" type="x-p"/>

Greek, "Faithful is the saying."<div eID="gen37642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37643" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">For--</hi>"For" the fact is so that, "if we be dead with Him (the Greek aorist tense implies a state once for all entered into in past times at the moment of regeneration, <reference osisRef="Rom.6.3">Ro 6:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.4.8">4, 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.12">Col 2:12</reference>), we shall also live with Him." The symmetrical form of "the saying," <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.11-2Tim.2.13">2Ti 2:11-13</reference>, and the rhythmical balance of the parallel clauses, makes it likely, they formed part of a Church hymn (see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1Ti 3:16</reference>), or accepted formula, perhaps first uttered by some of the Christian "prophets" in the public assembly (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.26">1Co 14:26</reference>). The phrase "faithful is the saying," which seems to have been the usual formula (compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.15">1Ti 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.1">3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.9">4:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.3.8">Tit 3:8</reference>) in such cases, favors this. <div eID="gen37643" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 11. Greek, "Faithful is the saying." The symmetrical form of "the saying," 2Ti 2:11-13 , and the rhythmical balance of the parallel clauses, makes it likely, they formed part of a Church hymn (see on 1Ti 3:16 ), or accepted formula, perhaps first uttered by some of the Christian "prophets" in the public assembly ( 1Co 14:26 ). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18204"/><div sID="gen37674" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18204"/><hi type="bold">19. Nevertheless--</hi>Notwithstanding the subversion of their faith, "the firm foundation of God standeth" fast (so the Greek ought to be translated). The "foundation" here is "the Church" [Alford], "the ground" or basement support "of the truth" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.15">1Ti 3:15</reference>), Christ Himself being the ultimate "foundation" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.3.11">1Co 3:11</reference>). In the steadfast standing of the Church there is involved the steadfast certainty of the doctrine in question (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.18">2Ti 2:18</reference>). Thus the "house" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.20">2Ti 2:20</reference>) answers to the "foundation"; it is made up of the elect whom "the Lord knoweth" (acknowledgeth, recognizes, <reference osisRef="Ps.1.6">Psa 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.7.23">Mt 7:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.10.14">Joh 10:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.3">1Co 8:3</reference>) as "His," and who persevere to the end, though others "err concerning the faith" (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.24">Mt 24:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.10.28">Joh 10:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.38">Ro 8:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.39">39</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.19">1Jo 2:19</reference>). Bengel takes "the foundation" to be the immovable faithfulness of God (to His promises to His elect [Calvin]). This contrasts well with the erring from the faith on the part of the reprobate, <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.18">2Ti 2:18</reference>. Though they deny the faith, God abates not His faithfulness (compare <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.13">2Ti 2:13</reference>).<div eID="gen37674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37675" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">having--</hi>seeing that it has [Ellicott].<div eID="gen37675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37676" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seal--</hi>"inscription": indicating ownership and destination: inscriptions were often engraven on a "foundation" stone (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.14">Re 21:14</reference>) [Alford]. This will agree with the view that "the foundation" is the Church (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.20">Ep 2:20</reference>). If it be taken God's immovable faithfulness, the "seal" will be regarded as attached to His covenant promise, with the inscription or legend, on one side of its round surface, "The Lord knoweth (it is 'knew' in the Septuagint, <reference osisRef="Num.16.5">Nu 16:5</reference>, to which Paul here alludes, altering it for his purpose by the Spirit) them that are His"; on the observe side, "Let every one that nameth (as his Lord, <reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Psa 20:7</reference>, or preacheth in His name, <reference osisRef="Jer.20.9">Jr 20:9</reference>) Christ."<div eID="gen37676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37677" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">depart--</hi>Greek, "stand aloof."<div eID="gen37677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37678" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from iniquity--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.52.11">Is 52:11</reference>). In both clauses there may be an allusion to <reference osisRef="Num.16.5">Nu 16:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.16.26">26</reference>, Septuagint. God's part and man's part are marked out. God chooseth and knoweth His elect; our part is to believe, and by the Spirit depart from all iniquity, an unequivocal proof of our being the Lord's (compare <reference osisRef="Deut.29.29">De 29:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.13.23-Luke.13.27">Lu 13:23-27</reference>). St. Lucian when asked by his persecutors, "Of what country art thou?" replied, "I am a Christian." "What is your occupation? ... I am a Christian." "Of what family? ... I am a Christian." [Chrysostom, Orations, 75]. He cannot be honored with the name Christian, who dishonors by iniquity, Christ, the Author of the name. However, different Greek pronouns stand for "him" and "his"; and the Greek for "taken captive" means not "captured for destruction," but "for being saved alive," as in Lu 5:10 , "Thou shalt catch men to save them unto life"; also there is no article before the Greek participle, which the English Version "who are taken captive," would require. Therefore, translate, "That they may awake ... taken as saved (and willing) captives by him (the servant of the Lord, 2Ti 2:24 ), so as to follow the will of HIM (the Lord, 2Ti 2:24 , or "God," 2Ti 2:25 )." There are here two evils, the "snare" and sleep, from which they are delivered: and two goods to which they are translated, awaking and deliverance. Instead of Satan's thrall comes the free and willing captivity of obedience to Christ ( 2Co 10:5 ). It is God who goes before, giving repentance ( 2Ti 2:25 ); then the work of His servant following is sure to be crowned with success, leading the convert henceforth to "live to the will of God" ( Ac 22:14 ; 1Pe 4:2 ).
